reader.title: Threatened lynching of John Andrew Johnson
bases: Crowds at Crockett were reported to intend to take Johnson from jail and lynch him, in June and again in October 1888, but he was guarded, tried and legally hanged (A1, A3, A7).

A mob of 'indignant citizens' was reported demanding Johnson to lynch him on a rape accusation (A3), but no one was killed by the mob; Johnson was tried, sentenced and executed by the state on Dec. 21 (A6, A7). This is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.

Houston and Austin dispatches report armed guards and a threatening mob at the Crockett jail (A1, A3, A4), but a Crockett correspondent said the Austin report was 'rather mixed' and that there was never any occasion for troops (A5).

summary.text: The threatened lynching of John Andrew Johnson took place in Crockett, Houston County, Texas, in 1888, when crowds sought to take the Black youth from jail while he awaited trial on a charge of raping a white girl.
An Austin dispatch of October 11 described a large mob besieging the jail and the governor sending the adjutant general, but a Crockett correspondent called that account mistaken.
Johnson was not lynched; he was tried, sentenced to death, and hanged by the state on December 21.
According to a Crockett report published after the execution, Miss Allie Simms, about seventeen, was assaulted and raped on June 13, 1888, near her father's home about six miles from Crockett.
Johnson, described as a colored youth of about nineteen, was arrested on the charge and jailed at Crockett.
The same report said "it was well known that many intended to take the law in their own hands" and hang him, so the sheriff moved him "by stratagem" to the Harris County jail.
Johnson spent about two months in the jail at Houston before Sheriff Ellis took him back to Crockett on October 5 for the fall term of the district court.
On his return the next morning, Ellis told a Houston reporter that the citizens of Crockett were "very indignant" and that sixteen armed men were guarding the jail to prevent a lynching.

A special dispatch from Austin dated October 11 went further, reporting that "a large and threatening mob of indignant citizens" surrounded the jail and loudly demanded the prisoner, whom it called "Young Johnson."
In that account the sheriff barricaded the jail and, with eleven men armed with Winchesters, refused to give up the prisoner and telegraphed the governor for aid.
Governor Ross ordered Adjutant General King to Crockett, and King left by that night's train.
Johnson was tried in the district court at Crockett on October 18, and the jury returned a death verdict after about forty minutes.
The court of appeals affirmed the judgment, and he was hanged at Crockett on December 21 before a crowd estimated at 3,000, "mostly colored."
He maintained to the end that the girl had mistaken him and that the colored boy who testified against him had lied.
No arrests of anyone in the crowds appear in the coverage.

Coverage was confined to Texas papers, and most of it ran in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, which printed the Houston dispatch, the Austin special, a Crockett rebuttal, and reports of the trial and hanging.
The Austin Weekly Statesman reprinted the Houston item under the headline "Threatened With Lynching," and the San Antonio Daily Light condensed the Austin news into a one-line state brief.
The early dispatches reported the threat without comment, quoting the guards' view that "the law must be respected and upheld at all cost."
Reports from Crockett itself took a different tone, calling Johnson "the rapist" before his trial and heading the verdict story "A Rape Fiend to Hang."
The December account said all approved "the vindication of the law" and stressed that the accuser was of good family and the jury among the best citizens.

The Crockett correspondent wrote on October 15 that the Austin correspondent "got things rather mixed," that Johnson had not yet been tried, and that no troops had been sent nor had there ever been any occasion to send any.
In his telling, Johnson's return caused only "a ripple of excitement" involving some young men of the neighborhood, but the surviving text breaks off at that point.
The local trial reports support his correction on the conviction date, while the Houston report of sixteen guards and the later Crockett history confirm that a lynching was feared.

accounts.label: Houston dispatch (Sheriff Ellis)
accounts.gist: Crockett citizens were 'very indignant' when Johnson was returned, and sixteen armed men guarded the jail to prevent a lynching.

accounts.label: Austin dispatch
accounts.gist: A large, growing mob surrounded the jail demanding 'Young Johnson', said to have been convicted the day before; the sheriff and eleven men barricaded it and the governor sent the adjutant general.

accounts.label: Crockett correspondent
accounts.gist: The Austin account was 'rather mixed': Johnson was awaiting trial, no troops were sent or needed, and his return caused only a 'ripple of excitement'.

accounts.label: Crockett report on the execution
accounts.gist: After the June arrest many intended to take Johnson from jail and hang him, so the sheriff moved him to Harris county; he was later tried, convicted and hanged.

framing.detail: The Houston and Austin dispatches reported the threat without comment, while quoting the guards that 'the law must be respected and upheld at all cost'.
Crockett reports called Johnson 'the rapist' and 'A Rape Fiend' before and after trial, played down the mob, and praised the hanging as 'the vindication of the law'.
